posts.title: Ruth and Daniel's three mornings at the window
posts.excerpt: Ruth and Daniel came for their 40th anniversary and moved their chairs to the window every morning.
posts.content:
Ruth and Daniel came to the Weir Room for three nights to mark their fortieth wedding anniversary. They arrived on a Thursday at four, in time for tea on the river terrace, and Jonas walked them along the bank to the weir before the light went.

On the first morning they sat where the table was set for them, with their backs to the room. On the second they asked Marta if they could turn their chairs to face the window, and on the third nobody needed to ask: the two chairs were already there, facing the water, with the board of bread and the jam from Lotte's orchard between them.

Marta sliced Ana's loaf at the kitchen window each morning while they ate. 'We moved our chairs to the window every morning,' Ruth wrote in the visitors' book, and underneath, in Daniel's hand: 'and we would again.' The Weir Room is on the first floor, with a king bed and a bay window over the water.

posts.title: Walking the weir path at four
posts.excerpt: Every afternoon at 16:00 Jonas walks the bank to the weir, 2.4 km in about forty minutes on a flat path.
posts.content:
At four o'clock Jonas puts down the tea towel and walks to the end of the garden, where the path along the bank begins. Anyone staying in the house may come. The walk to the weir is 2.4 km, flat all the way, and takes about forty minutes if nobody stops to look at the heron, which somebody always does.

In autumn the mist lies on the water until well after breakfast and lifts from the far bank first. Jonas knows where the alders lean over the path and where the bank is soft after rain, and he draws the route on the back of a menu for anyone who would rather go alone.

The walk ends at the weir, where the river drops half a metre and makes the sound the house is named after. Most people stand there for a while and then walk back in the lower light, in time for the lamps.

posts.title: Rowing out with Karim
posts.excerpt: From May to September Karim Haddad lends a wooden rowing boat from the mill pond jetty to guests of the house.
posts.content:
Karim Haddad keeps the rowing boats at the mill pond, a ten-minute walk upstream from the house. From May to September he lends one to any guest who asks, free of charge, with a life vest from the boathouse and a short lesson in how not to go in circles.

The Okafor family took a boat out on their second afternoon. The children rowed, badly, and their parents steered, worse, and they came back an hour later with wet sleeves and a handful of watercress that Karim told them was safe to eat.

Ask Marta when you write about dates if you would like a boat on a particular afternoon; Karim likes a day's notice, and the pond is calmest before eleven.
